newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea banks to compete under rate deregulation.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea banks to compete under rate deregulation.

text.p: South Korea's latest round of interest rate deregulation would push up some savings rates and spark fierce competition within the banking industry, analysts said on Thursday.
The central Bank of Korea (BOK), announcing the fourth stage of rate liberalisation, said it would allow banks to set their own interest rates on savings accounts from July 7.
BOK also said it would allow banks to introduce money market deposit accounts and issue three-year bonds.

"The announcement will remove big obstacles in the domestic banking business. Banks are expected to enter an era of full-scale competition," said Scott Seo, banking analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Capital Markets Ltd.
"This signalled even banks could go bust, if they mismanaged interest rates," he said.
BOK director Park Cheul told reporters: "The competition will promote liberalisation of the financial industry from a longer point of view."
Interest rates on savings accounts for individuals, into which many South Korean employees have their salaries directly deposited, would also be liberalised.
Under current regulations, South Korean banks have set their annual interest rate on savings accounts at three percent.
Deregulation was good news for some South Korean banks and bad news for others.
"From a price effect point of veiw, it's not good news for larger banks as it will lower their margins," said Kim Chul-jung, banking analyst at Ssangyong Securities.
But he said newer bankers such as Shinhan Bank, Hana Bank and Boram Bank would raise their rates to six percent to secure a more stable source of funding.
Hana Bank spokesman Yoo Cha-yul said the bank was considering raising its rates to attract deposits.
Analysts said such deposits accounted for almost 20 percent of total bank savings. For Kookmin Bank, the amount reached six trillion won ($6.76 billion).
Seo at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said a three percent increase in the savings rate would reduce Kookmin Bank's earnings per share by 1,000 won.

"Major banks would not raise their rates," Lee In-hyung, analyst at LG Economic Research Institute, said. "Today's announcement contained no surprising news as it had been already planned. I believe many banks already prepared to cushion any shocks."
An official at Korea First Bank bemoaned the deregulation news, saying an increase of one percentage point in the bank's rates would reduce its profits by 30 billion won.
"It's very regrettable to see the announcement, especially when the domestic banking industry faces difficulties from a slew of debt defaults by big companies," he said.

To offset possible losses and hone a competitive edge, banks would be allowed to introduce market-sensitive money market deposit accounts, which would offer interest rates comparable to money market rates.
Depositors would be able to withdraw their money on demand and interest rates would normally be higher.
To raise the funding capability of banks, the central bank said it would allow them to issue three-year bonds. But the amount would be limited to no more than 50 percent of the bank's equity capital.
The central bank forecast bonds issued by banks would total 4.8 trillion won over the next year, compared to South Korea's total estimated bond issues of 36 trillion won for this year.
All demand deposit rates, including those on passbook, checking and household accounts, would be liberalised after January 1, 1998. ($1 = 887.40)
